clue.text: Chief priest ran distractedly round church fire

indicators.note: round says the jumbled letters go around the other pieces like a ring
a person acting distractedly is all over the place, so these letters lose their order

parts.note: taken as written, then jumbled
CH is the usual abbreviation for church
a flame is fire

explanation.surface: A senior cleric panics and runs about as the church burns.
explanation.walkthrough: A flamen was a priest of one Roman god; the jumbled letters split in two to wrap around the other pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: An archflamen was a chief flamen, the head priest of a Roman deity's cult.

clue.text: Where vermin lurk, later running round house

indicators.note: round says the shuffled letters encircle the next piece
running suggests the letters are in motion and settle in a new order

parts.note: taken as written, then rearranged
HO is the standard abbreviation for house

explanation.surface: Pests hide somewhere, and later scamper about the house.
explanation.definitionFit: A rathole is a rodent's burrow or a squalid den, a hiding place for rats.

clue.text: I briefly put in call for nuts

indicators.note: put in means placed inside another word

parts.note: a cry is a call

indicators.note: briefly means the setter's name is cut short at its end

parts.note: I is the setter, whose pen name is Azed

explanation.surface: The speaker admits briefly making a call about nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: In a puzzle 'I' can mean its setter; this setter's pen name is Azed, which loses its last two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Both nuts and crazy are informal words for mad, so the adjective swaps cleanly.

clue.text: Reconstructed neolith establishing special link

indicators.note: something reconstructed is rebuilt from its parts in a new shape

parts.note: a stone-age implement, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Archaeologists rebuild an ancient stone monument and discover it was a special link.
explanation.definitionFit: A hotline is a direct dedicated telephone connection, for instance between heads of government.

clue.text: Atmosphere in crowded tavern, chilliness restricting women?

indicators.note: restricting means holding something in, so one piece is enclosed by another

parts.note: frost is a chill in the air
W is the abbreviation for women

explanation.surface: A packed pub has a strange chill, perhaps because the women are kept out.
explanation.definitionFit: Frowst is a hot, stale, stuffy air, the kind found in a packed, unventilated bar.

clue.text: What can come into the equation when goddess replaces ham in The Palace?

definitions.text: What can come into the equation

indicators.note: replaces says one part of a word is swapped out for another

parts.note: the Alhambra is the famous Moorish palace in Granada
taken as written, the part removed
Ge, or Gaia, is the Greek earth goddess

explanation.surface: A puzzle about swapping a goddess for a ham actor in a palace, posed as a riddle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Come into the equation' is an idiom for being relevant, but here it is literal: algebra is the stuff of equations.
explanation.definitionFit: Algebra is the branch of mathematics using symbols, which is what fills an equation.

clue.text: Damage on parapet, part removed? This may check erosion

indicators.note: part removed tells us to take away the word part itself from the longer word
on in a down clue places the first part above the second

parts.note: to mar is to damage
a rampart is a defensive parapet

explanation.surface: Damage to a wall has taken part of it away; something should check the erosion.
explanation.definitionFit: Marram is a coarse grass planted on dunes because its roots bind sand against wind erosion.

clue.text: Seine below island in city? Increasing numbers reach it nowadays

indicators.note: in says the pieces sit inside the city's abbreviation

parts.note: NY is New York

indicators.note: below in a down clue sets one piece under another

parts.note: I is the abbreviation for island
a seine is a large fishing net, not the French river

explanation.surface: A query about the river Seine and an island in Paris, then a remark on growing numbers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seine' looks like the Paris river, but here it is a fishing net.
explanation.definitionFit: More people now live to the age of ninety, a milestone age reached in increasing numbers.

clue.text: A feature of Dante's tropes?

indicators.note: a feature of means a part of, so the answer is sitting within the following words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the poet's name and the start of the next word

explanation.surface: A literary question about what marks the Italian poet's figures of speech.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is also the definition: estro is poetic fervour, a feature of Dante's writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Estro is an Italian word for creative enthusiasm or poetic inspiration, apt for Dante's imagery.

clue.text: Trap Shane set spinning yard — wherein game'll get started

indicators.note: set spinning means whirled about until the letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken letter for letter, then jumbled
Y is the abbreviation for yard

explanation.surface: Someone sets up a trap for Shane in a yard where a game begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' is not a sport but game birds, which are reared before the shooting begins.
explanation.definitionFit: A pheasantry is a place where pheasants are bred and reared, so the game birds start life there.

clue.text: Virgil's family recipe for a bitter dish

parts.note: Maro was the family name of the Roman poet Publius Vergilius Maro
R is the abbreviation for recipe, as on prescriptions

explanation.surface: A poet's family passes down a recipe for a bitter dish.
explanation.definitionFit: Maror are the bitter herbs eaten at the Passover Seder, recalling the bitterness of slavery.

clue.text: Slick scheme the Scots issue

parts.note: a plan is a scheme
ish is a Scots legal word for issue or expiry

explanation.surface: A smooth plan is put out by the Scots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slick' reads as an adjective but is a verb: to make smooth.
explanation.definitionFit: To planish is to flatten and polish metal by hammering, so to make it sleek.

clue.text: Non-mover with spinner in touch cuts like this and runs

indicators.note: cuts means slicing into the next word, so one piece goes inside it

parts.note: so means in this way
tat is a light touch or tap
R is the abbreviation for runs in cricket scoring

explanation.surface: Instructions for a machine part or a cricket shot played like this for runs.
explanation.definitionFit: A stator is the fixed part of an electric motor or turbine, set against the rotating rotor.

clue.text: Junior, passionate about nothing, rarely twitching

definitions.note: rarely flags that this is an uncommon word

parts.note: a sub is a subordinate or junior

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one word wraps around a letter

parts.note: sultry means sensual or passionate
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: A young person, passionate about nothing, hardly ever moves a muscle.
explanation.definitionFit: Subsultory is a rare adjective for moving in sudden jerks or starts, that is, twitching.

clue.text: Old scallywag making name in early fiddle

indicators.note: making here means putting a piece into another to form something, so it sits inside

parts.note: a rote was a medieval stringed instrument
N is the abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A historic rascal makes a name for himself on an early violin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' hints at cheating to suit 'scallywag', but here it is an old instrument, the rote.
explanation.definitionFit: Ronte is Spenser's form of runt, used in old writing as a term of contempt for a wretch or rogue.

clue.text: Bad gardener's bungled and this composite died

indicators.note: bungled means botched or mixed up, so the letters are jumbled

parts.note: taken letter for letter as the jumbled whole
taken as written, letters accounted for in the jumble
D is the abbreviation for died

explanation.surface: A poor gardener mishandled things and this flower died.
explanation.walkthrough: A composite anagram: BAD GARDENER is a mix of AND, the answer, and D, so take AND and D out of its letters to leave the flower.
explanation.definitionFit: The gerbera is a daisy-like plant of the Compositae family, botanically a composite.

clue.text: Youthful mistake involving love, unknown

indicators.note: involving means wrapping around, so other letters are taken inside

parts.note: bish is British slang for a blunder
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O
Y is an algebraic unknown

explanation.surface: A youthful error involving romance with a stranger.
explanation.definitionFit: Boyish means like a boy, so young-looking or juvenile in manner, a near synonym for youthful.

clue.text: Top clubs, needing forward, fish around

indicators.note: around says one word encircles another

parts.note: the bass is a fish
to means forward, as in to and fro

explanation.surface: Elite golf clubs need a forward player and a fish nearby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top clubs' is the plural of basto, the ace of clubs in the old card games ombre and quadrille.
explanation.definitionFit: In ombre the basto is the highest-ranking club, so bastos are top clubs in card terms.

clue.text: Changing sterling loses grand — it's an Aussie dodge

indicators.note: changing means altering the order, so the letters are rearranged
loses says a letter is taken out of the word

parts.note: taken as written
G is short for a grand, a thousand pounds

explanation.surface: Converting British money costs a thousand: a classic Australian swindle.
explanation.definitionFit: Slinter is Australian slang for a trick or ruse, which is a dodge.

clue.text: Old servant pinching the sauce? There's a legal excuse

indicators.note: pinching means gripping something tight, so one word holds another inside

parts.note: an esne was an Anglo-Saxon labourer or slave
soy is a sauce

explanation.surface: A servant of old is caught stealing the sauce and pleads a legal excuse.
explanation.definitionFit: An essoyne, or essoin, was an excuse for not appearing in court, a formal legal plea.

clue.text: Damper indoors? That's silly

indicators.note: silly means foolish or messed up, so the letters are in a nonsensical order

parts.note: taken letter for letter, then rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a wet spell keeps people inside, and calls it silly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Damper' suggests wetter weather, but it is a device that softens sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A sordino is a mute for a stringed or brass instrument, which damps its tone.

clue.text: Worrying development in Blackpool for entertainer there?

parts.note: Blackpool is a seaside resort famous for its piers
rot is decay, a worrying development in an old structure

explanation.surface: A troubling event at a British seaside resort affects its performers.
explanation.walkthrough: Blackpool is a resort in north-west England; decay in its pier is pier rot, and a pierrot is a clown who played end-of-pier shows.
explanation.definitionFit: A pierrot is a white-faced clown, a type of performer common in seaside pier shows.

clue.text: President mostly imbibing southern wine

indicators.note: imbibing means drinking in, so one letter goes inside
mostly means most but not all, so the final letter is dropped

parts.note: Barack Obama, the US president
S is the abbreviation for southern

explanation.surface: A president, nearly drunk, sips a southern wine.
explanation.definitionFit: Barsac is a sweet white wine from the Bordeaux region of France.

clue.text: Like many gas meters you'll find through entering confined space

indicators.note: entering means going inside, so one word sits within another

parts.note: a coop is a small cramped enclosure
in can mean through, as in 'in that way'

explanation.surface: Old gas meters are reached by squeezing into a cramped cupboard.
explanation.walkthrough: Coin-op is short for coin-operated; many British homes once had gas meters fed with coins.
explanation.definitionFit: Coinop means coin-operated, the way prepayment gas meters used to work.

clue.text: Frothy glucoside hospital accepts in operation? The reverse

indicators.note: accepts means taking in, so one word holds another

parts.note: a san is a sanatorium

indicators.note: the reverse says the order of the inserted words must be turned around

parts.note: taken as written
OP is short for operation

explanation.surface: A hospital admits a patient in surgery, or the other way about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The reverse' flips IN OP, which then goes into SAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Saponins are plant glucosides that foam in water, so a frothy glucoside is an example of one.

clue.text: What visitors climb to reach front door (and not salesperson turning up)

definitions.text: What visitors climb to reach front door

indicators.note: in a down clue turning up means read upwards, so the order is flipped

parts.note: nor means and not
a rep is a sales representative

explanation.surface: Visitors climb steps to the front door, but not the salesperson who turns up.
explanation.definitionFit: A perron is an external flight of steps leading to the entrance of a large building.

clue.text: What'll set everyone back: not one special, just endless plains!

indicators.note: set back means placed backwards, so the word runs right to left

parts.note: all means everyone
no means not one
S is the abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: An exclamation about costly scenery: nothing special, just mile upon mile of grassland.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set everyone back' looks like a cost, but it reverses ALL.
explanation.definitionFit: The llanos are the vast treeless grassland plains of northern South America.

clue.text: Learner works without a desk-top support

parts.note: L is the learner plate

indicators.note: without means lacking, so a letter is taken away

parts.note: opera is the plural of opus, a work
taken as written, the letter removed

explanation.surface: A trainee is working without a support for his desk top.
explanation.definitionFit: A loper is a sliding rail that pulls out to hold up the fall-front writing flap of a bureau.

clue.text: Compound used as pigment — some never deteriorates

indicators.note: some means a portion of, so the answer is part of the words that follow

parts.note: letters run over the end of the first word into the second

explanation.surface: A pigment compound claims that some paint never fades.
explanation.definitionFit: Verdet is neutral copper acetate, a verdigris compound used as a green pigment.

clue.text: Indian cotton, creased — hot iron circumvents that

indicators.note: circumvents means goes around, so these words surround and hold the answer

parts.note: the last letter of the first word, the whole second word, and the first letter of the third

explanation.surface: A creased cotton garment from India, which a hot iron goes round.
explanation.walkthrough: 'that' points back to the answer: the creased cloth is what the hot iron goes around.
explanation.definitionFit: A dhoti is a Hindu loincloth, and also the coarse cotton cloth it is made of.

clue.text: Strain, the ultimate for downcast Orsino, distraught

indicators.note: the ultimate means the very last, so only the closing letter is kept

parts.note: the final letter of the word

indicators.note: distraught means deeply upset, so the letters are in turmoil

parts.note: the lovesick duke of Twelfth Night, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's sad, frantic Duke Orsino is under great strain.
explanation.definitionFit: Torsion is twisting stress applied to an object, a kind of mechanical strain.

clue.text: Component of visual purple you'll need because of following other people's

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the first piece listed goes at the end

parts.note: OPs is slang for other people's, especially cigarettes cadged from others
in can mean because of, as in 'in that'

explanation.surface: A purple pigment requires borrowing from others.
explanation.walkthrough: Visual purple is rhodopsin, the light-sensitive pigment of the eye's rods.
explanation.definitionFit: Opsin is the protein part of rhodopsin, combined with retinal to form the pigment.

clue.text: Religious community — it's lost out in preference

indicators.note: lost out means dropped from the word, so those letters vanish

parts.note: priority is precedence or preference
taken as written, the letters to remove

explanation.surface: A monastic group has lost out to a competing priority.
explanation.definitionFit: A priory is a monastery or convent run by a prior or prioress, a religious community.

clue.text: Debates about getting on in the law, famously?

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: in places the word inside another

parts.note: Mr Bumble in Oliver Twist famously said the law is an ass
taken as written

explanation.surface: Lawyers argue about progress in the famous law.
explanation.definitionFit: To reason is to argue or discuss logically, so reasons means debates as a verb.

clue.text: Following breakdown lorry in Luton Town? (5, two words)

indicators.note: in means inside, so the answer lies within the words after it

parts.note: the letters span the two words of the football club's name

explanation.surface: A car is pulled by a recovery truck in a Bedfordshire town.
explanation.walkthrough: Luton is a town north of London; Luton Town is its football club.
explanation.definitionFit: A car on tow is being pulled behind another vehicle, such as a recovery lorry after a breakdown.

clue.text: Scotsman's drunk an aperitif (not the last) in e.g. Paris

definitions.note: the Scots adjective sense, heady or giddy with drink

indicators.note: in places one group inside the city word

parts.note: Paris is an example of a city
the indefinite article

indicators.note: not the last means dropping the final letter

parts.note: Pernod is an aniseed aperitif

explanation.surface: A Scotsman has had a French aperitif in Paris and is tipsy.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots capernoity, from the head or noddle, also means muddled or heady, as when tipsy.
